terms.grammar: adjective (participle of frangō, frangere, frēgī, frāctum)
evidence: Cato Agr. 144: nisi quae vetustāte frāctae erunt
Caes. BG 4.29.3: complūribus nāvibus frāctīs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: “It’s broken” is frāctum est; “who broke it?”, quis frēgit? Broken into little pieces is comminūtus (see break into pieces); a string or a balloon that has burst is ruptus (see burst); a broken bone, see fracture.

terms.grammar: phrase; in the perfect, vitium fēcit
evidence: Cic. Top. 15: sī aedēs corruērunt vitiumve fēcērunt (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Cicero’s phrase for a house that has been damaged. For a machine that has stopped working it is our suggestion.

phrases.latin: scālae ita utī datae erunt, ita redditō, nisi quae vetustāte frāctae erunt
phrases.english: return the ladders as they were given, except any that have broken with age

phrases.latin: frangere dum metuis, frangēs crystallina: peccant sēcūrae nimium sollicitaeque manūs
phrases.english: while you are afraid of breaking the glass, you will break it: hands that are too careless slip, and so do hands that are too careful

fractus.html: De Vaan 239, s.v. frangō: “The long vowel of fractus is due to Lachmann’s Law.” Traupman 106 marks it too.

sources: Lewis & Short: frango · Lewis & Short: vitium
